abstract.p: This elegy mourns Queen Anne as a uniquely virtuous figure whose death has deprived the kingdom of both its joy and its moral exemplar. The speaker commemorates her as the ‘bright protectresse of disgrac't desart’. Death is personified as a tyrant, compared to Nero and hailed as the ‘conquerour of Albion’ for having taken both Anne and her ‘matchlesse sonne’. The poem repeatedly elevates Anne above ordinary human virtue, describing her as ‘Vertue impersonated’ and arguing that her departure must therefore provoke universal grief. While her death is acknowledged as a heavenly ‘advancement’, the speaker interprets the loss suffered by the living as ‘our sinnes just crosse’. The closing lines unite the figures of Astraea and Virtue, suggesting that Anne’s death marks the departure from earth of both justice and virtue themselves.

div.head: An Elegie on the death of Queene Anne

lg.l: Pay tribute eyes, she's gone, one her attend
Virtues best meritt, and our joyes, whose end
Began with her disease, you that are good
And wisely feele her losse, knowing she stood
The bright protectresse of disgrac't desart:
Mourne and grow stupid, weepe not eyes but heart,
Such greifes as these are truelier felt then uttred,
So swan-lik farewell's, are not spoke but muttred.
Death thou to Nero-like dost sek Deale thy darts,
For with this stroake th'hast peirc't a thousand hearts:
Her losse, wanne tyrant, with her matchlesse sonne
Have stil'd thee conquerour of Albion
None now resist thy power, nor gainst thee strive,
For who (they dying) would not scorne to live?
This is greifes essence, he had never worth,
That now can stop his sighs from renting forth
See how the cloud's weepe still, and shall not I
Who onely live to t'adore her memory?
Vertue impersonated need's must raise,
Say ould Phylosopher's the love and praise,
Of each admiring veiwer, must not then
Her separation worke most greife in men?
O and in Angell's to, save that they gaine
By her accessse, perfectiion to their traine.
Pardon (sweet Angell) that wee thy losse,
Though thy advancement, twas our sinnes just crosse,
But since Astraeas fled, and Vertue's gone,
Why should she best and greatest stay alone.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Anne of Denmark, queen consort of James I, died unexpectedly on 2 March 1619 at Hampton Court after a period of ill health. Her death prompted a wave of elegiac writing that, while less intense than that following the death of her son, Prince Henry, nonetheless reflects broader national anxieties and the developing conventions of mourning royal figures in the early Stuart period.(Doelman 2016)

Doelman (2016, 101) cites Sir Sampson Darell's elegy among others which pay tribute to Anne's assistance to outsiders or those who had lost favour at court. ‘Helpe the helpless side’ as one poem puts it.
